newsitem.title: USA: U.S. leaves open possible new Iraq strikes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. leaves open possible new Iraq strikes.

text.p: The CIA said on Thursday that Iraqi troops were leaving northern Iraq, but the Clinton Administration said they remained a threat and refused to rule out new U.S. attacks on President Saddam Hussein's forces.

As U.S. warplanes kept watch on an expanded no-fly zone in southern Iraq for the second day, John Deutch, director of the Central Intelligence Agency, said heavy Iraqi units were pulling out of the Western-protected Kurdish safe haven they had punched into over the weekend.

"We are seeing the withdrawal of the mechanized and armored units from the Kurdish territories in northern Iraq back to their garrisons fairly systematically," Deutch said in testimony before the Senate Intelligence Committee. Later, he told students at Georgetown University that elements of seven divisions that had been in the north had returned to barracks.

But State Department spokesman Glyn Davies cautioned against taking a narrow view of Iraqi deployments, saying that Saddam had introduced a "massive security presence" in the Kurdish area under cover of troop deployments.

"So his troops remain very much a threat to Iraq's civilian population in the north. And we will continue to assess that threat, and indeed the threat elsewhere in Iraq, as we decide on U.S. actions," Davies said.

Defense Secretary William Perry said U.S. forces reserved the right to strike Iraq again if it tries to rebuild air defenses in the south disabled by a total of 44 U.S. cruise missiles fired this week.
"We are reserving the right to go back again if we need to go back again," Perry said in an interview on CNN. "If they threaten our airplanes they will be inviting additional problems."

Perry said the Iraqis appeared to be leaving security forces, including secret police and infantry, in the Kurdish-populated northern city of Arbil. The city was seized by one Kurdish faction with the help of Iraqi troops from a rival group on Saturday.

Saddam has vowed to ignore the exclusion zones in both northern and southern Iraq, where they have been enforced by allied warplanes since the aftermath of the 1991 Gulf War that ousted his invasion forces from Kuwait.
Deutch, in his remarks at Georgetown University, said he did not think Saddam had "an easy and immediate way to respond" to the U.S. strikes.
He said that Iraq, with or without Saddam Hussein, would continue to be a problem and could pose future threats not only to the Kurds but to oil-rich neighbors like Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.
"It's not only Saddam Hussein, it's the regime that he's part of, the immediate group that he's part of," Deutch said.

Although President Bill Clinton claimed on Wednesday that the cruise missile strikes had taught Saddam a necessary lesson, two senior members of Congress said on Thursday Clinton might have to resume such attacks to drive the lesson home.
"Saddam has not been discouraged by our attacks," Republican Senator Richard Lugar of Indiana said in an interview on Fox television.
"We are going to have to do more to get the word across to him ... make certain that he is badly crippled, that his military instruments are crippled."
Democratic Representative Lee Hamilton of Indiana concurred with that view in the same interview. "I certainly think additional power may be necessary here against Saddam Hussein," he said.
Lugar and Hamilton are two of the more influential foreign policy voices in their respective houses of Congress.
